topics.name: Physical Chemistry
concepts: Oxidation number: sum = charge; O is −2 (except peroxides −1, OF₂ +2), H is +1 (−1 in metal hydrides) [repeat]
Order = sum of powers in the experimental rate law; may be zero or fractional; molecularity is always a whole number [repeat]
Graham's law: r ∝ 1/√M, so r(H₂) : r(O₂) = 4 : 1 [repeat]
Surface tension and viscosity of a liquid decrease as temperature rises; liquids boil at lower temperature at high altitude [repeat]
Unit cell atoms: corner 1/8, face 1/2, body 1; simple cubic 1, bcc 2, fcc 4 [repeat]
Number of orbitals in shell n = n²; electrons = 2n²; Aufbau order 3d → 4p → 5s [repeat]
Le Chatelier: high P favours fewer gas moles; heating favours the endothermic direction; a catalyst never shifts equilibrium [repeat]
First law: ΔU = q + w (conservation of energy); heat absorbed and work done on the system are positive [repeat]
Common ion lowers solubility: Mg(OH)₂ is least soluble in NaOH solution [repeat]
Limiting reagent is used up first; % N in urea = 28/60 × 100 = 46.7% [repeat]
Redox titration: 2MnO₄⁻ ≡ 5C₂O₄²⁻; KMnO₄ n-factor 5 in acid; ppm = (mass solute/mass solution) × 10⁶ [repeat]
H₂–O₂ fuel cell: anode H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻; product water [repeat]
First order: t½ = 0.693/k, independent of initial concentration; 99.9% completion ≈ 10 half-lives
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; ΔG° = −2.303RT log K; spontaneous at all T when ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0
pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C; buffer pH = pKa + log[salt]/[acid]; Ksp(AB₂) = 4s³
α decay: A − 4, Z − 2; β decay: Z + 1; γ: no change; C-14 t½ = 5730 years [repeat]

topics.name: Analytical Chemistry
concepts: Lassaigne's (sodium fusion) extract detects N, S and halogens; N gives Prussian blue, S gives violet with nitroprusside [repeat]
Baeyer's reagent = cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄; its pink colour is discharged by C=C or C≡C [repeat]
Terminal alkynes (ethyne) give red ppt with ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂ and white ppt with ammoniacal AgNO₃; ethene does not [repeat]
H₂S turns lead acetate paper black (PbS) [repeat]
Methyl orange: red in acid, yellow in base (range 3.1–4.4); phenolphthalein colourless in acid, pink in base (8.3–10) [repeat]
Indicator choice: strong acid–weak base → methyl orange; weak acid–strong base → phenolphthalein; weak–weak → none suitable
Victor Meyer test: 1° alcohol blood red, 2° blue, 3° colourless [repeat]
Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes, not ketones; Fehling's is not reduced by benzaldehyde [repeat]
Lucas test: 3° alcohol turbid at once, 2° in ~5 min, 1° no turbidity at room temperature
Biuret test → violet (protein); iodine → blue-black (starch); Sudan III → red (fat)
Cl⁻: white AgCl soluble in NH₄OH; SO₄²⁻: white BaSO₄ insoluble in HCl; NH₄⁺: brown ppt with Nessler's reagent
Sublimation separates camphor, naphthalene, iodine; vacuum distillation for liquids that decompose at their boiling point
Paper chromatography: Rf = distance moved by solute / distance moved by solvent (always < 1)
Iodimetry titrates directly with standard I₂; iodometry titrates liberated I₂ with hypo; starch is the indicator
KMnO₄ is a self-indicator; EDTA with Eriochrome Black T is used for complexometric (hardness) titration

questions.q: Number of molecules in 4.4 g of CO₂ is
Volume occupied by 8 g of O₂ at STP is
questions.trap: 11.2 L: taking O₂ molar mass as 16 g.

questions.q: 4 g of NaOH dissolved in water to make 500 mL solution. Its molarity is
questions.trap: 0.1 M: forgetting to convert 500 mL to 0.5 L.

questions.q: Equivalent weight of KMnO₄ (M = 158) in acidic medium is
questions.x: In acid MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺; n-factor 5, so 158/5 = 31.6.
questions.trap: 52.7 is for neutral medium (n-factor 3).

questions.q: Volume of 0.2 M NaOH needed to neutralise 25 mL of 0.1 M H₂SO₄ is
questions.trap: 12.5 mL: forgetting H₂SO₄ is dibasic.

questions.q: 2 g of H₂ reacts with 32 g of O₂ to form water. Mass of water formed is
questions.x: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 1 mol H₂ needs only 0.5 mol O₂, so H₂ is limiting: 1 mol H₂O = 18 g.
questions.trap: 34 g: simply adding the masses, ignoring excess O₂.

questions.q: A compound contains C 40%, H 6.67%, O 53.33%. Its empirical formula is
Maximum number of electrons in a subshell with l = 2 is
questions.x: Max electrons = 2(2l+1) = 2(5) = 10 (d subshell).

questions.q: Ground-state electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is
questions.x: One 4s electron shifts to 3d to give the extra-stable half-filled 3d⁵ set.
questions.trap: 3d⁴4s²: following the Aufbau order blindly.

questions.q: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, m, s) is NOT allowed?
questions.x: l can only be 0 to n−1; for n = 2, l cannot be 2.

questions.q: Number of radial and angular nodes in a 4d orbital are
questions.x: Radial = n − l − 1 = 4 − 2 − 1 = 1; angular = l = 2.
questions.trap: 2 radial: using n − l instead of n − l − 1.

questions.q: If the kinetic energy of an electron is made four times, its de Broglie wavelength becomes
questions.x: λ = h/√(2mK); K × 4 → √4 = 2, so λ becomes half.
questions.trap: One-fourth: forgetting the square root.

questions.q: Which has the highest first ionisation enthalpy?
questions.x: N has a stable half-filled 2p³ configuration, so its IE exceeds that of O.
questions.trap: O: assuming IE always increases across a period.

questions.q: Which element has the most negative electron gain enthalpy?
questions.x: In small F, added electron faces strong repulsion in the compact 2p shell, so Cl has the most negative value.
questions.trap: F: confusing electronegativity with electron gain enthalpy.

questions.q: Among the isoelectronic ions O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺, the smallest is
questions.x: All have 10 electrons; Mg²⁺ has the highest nuclear charge (12), pulling electrons closest.

questions.q: The shape of SF₄ is
questions.x: S: 4 bond pairs + 1 lone pair = sp³d; lone pair at equatorial position gives see-saw.
questions.trap: Tetrahedral: counting only the four bonds and ignoring the lone pair.
questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules

questions.q: Hybridisation of Xe in XeF₄ is
questions.x: Xe: 4 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs = 6 electron pairs → sp³d², square planar shape.
questions.trap: dsp²: square planar shape recalled from complexes like [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻.
questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules

questions.q: Bond order of O₂⁺ is
questions.x: O₂⁺ has 15 electrons; Nb = 10, Na = 5; bond order = (10 − 5)/2 = 2.5.
questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules

questions.q: Which molecule is paramagnetic?
questions.x: MOT gives O₂ two unpaired electrons in π* orbitals; the others have all electrons paired.
questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules

questions.q: Which molecule has zero dipole moment?
questions.x: BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical, so bond dipoles cancel.
questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules

questions.q: Which hydrogen halide has the highest boiling point?
questions.x: HF molecules are linked by strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
questions.trap: HI: expecting boiling point to rise with molar mass alone.
questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules

questions.q: Which pair has the same hybridisation of the central atom?
questions.x: N in NH₄⁺ and C in CH₄ are both sp³. BF₃ sp² vs NH₃ sp³; CO₂ sp vs SO₂ sp²; PCl₅ sp³d vs IF₅ sp³d².
questions.trap: CO₂ and SO₂: similar formula, but SO₂ has a lone pair.
questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules

questions.q: According to Fajans' rules, the most covalent chloride is
questions.x: Al³⁺ is small with high charge, so it polarises Cl⁻ most strongly.
questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules

questions.q: Ratio of rates of diffusion of H₂ to O₂ under the same conditions is
questions.trap: 16 : 1: forgetting the square root.

questions.q: Average kinetic energy of gas molecules is directly proportional to
questions.x: KE(avg) = (3/2)kT; it depends only on absolute temperature.

questions.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), the relation between Kp and Kc is
questions.x: Δn = 2 − 4 = −2, so Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn = Kc(RT)⁻².
questions.trap: Kp = Kc(RT)²: subtracting products from reactants.

questions.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH negative), the yield of NH₃ increases at
questions.x: Forward reaction reduces gas moles (favoured by high P) and is exothermic (favoured by low T).

questions.q: pH of 0.005 M Ba(OH)₂ solution is
questions.x: Ba(OH)₂ gives 2 OH⁻: [OH⁻] = 0.01 M, pOH = 2, pH = 14 − 2 = 12.
questions.trap: 11.7: forgetting the two OH⁻ per formula unit.

questions.q: Which mixture acts as a buffer?
questions.x: A buffer needs a weak acid with its salt of a strong base; the others contain strong acids/bases.

questions.q: Which is a Lewis acid?
questions.x: B in BF₃ has an incomplete octet and accepts an electron pair. The others donate lone pairs (Lewis bases).

questions.q: For a sparingly soluble salt AB₂ with solubility s mol/L, Ksp is
questions.x: AB₂ → A²⁺ + 2B⁻; Ksp = (s)(2s)² = 4s³.
questions.trap: 2s³: forgetting to square the 2.

questions.q: Standard enthalpy of formation is zero for
questions.x: ΔH°f is zero only for an element in its most stable standard state; O₂(g) is, while O₃ and diamond are not.
questions.trap: C(diamond): graphite, not diamond, is the standard form of carbon.

questions.q: For a reaction ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. It becomes spontaneous above
questions.trap: 0.4 K: not converting kJ to J.

questions.q: Unit of rate constant of a first-order reaction is
questions.x: For first order, k = rate/[A] = (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)/(mol L⁻¹) = s⁻¹.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has t½ = 10 min. Fraction of reactant left after 30 min is
questions.x: 30 min = 3 half-lives; fraction left = (½)³ = 1/8.

questions.q: Charge needed to deposit 27 g of Al from Al³⁺ is
questions.x: 27 g = 1 mol Al; Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al needs 3 F = 3 × 96500 = 289500 C.
questions.trap: 96500 C: forgetting the 3+ charge.

questions.q: Given E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, E°cell of the Daniell cell is
questions.x: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.
questions.trap: 0.42 V: subtracting magnitudes without signs.

questions.q: Percentage of nitrogen by mass in urea, CO(NH₂)₂, is
questions.trap: 23.3%: counting only one N atom.

questions.q: Hydrogen sulphide prepared by any method always contains H and S in the mass ratio 1 : 16. This illustrates the law of
questions.x: A pure compound always has the same elements combined in a fixed ratio by mass, whatever its source.
questions.trap: Multiple proportions needs two different compounds of the same elements.

questions.q: Carbon forms CO and CO₂. For a fixed mass of carbon, the masses of oxygen combined are in the ratio 1 : 2. This illustrates the law of
questions.x: Two compounds of the same two elements: masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio.

questions.q: 6 g of Mg is burnt in 8 g of O₂ (2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO). After the reaction the vessel contains
questions.x: 6 g Mg = 0.25 mol needs 0.125 mol O₂ = 4 g. Mg is limiting: MgO = 0.25 × 40 = 10 g; O₂ left = 8 − 4 = 4 g.
questions.trap: 14 g MgO: adding masses without finding the limiting reagent.

questions.q: One atomic mass unit (amu) is defined as
o: 1/16 of the mass of one oxygen-16 atom
1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom
questions.x: Since 1961 the reference standard is carbon-12: 1 amu = 1/12 × mass of a ¹²C atom = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

questions.q: Number of atoms in 11.2 L of N₂ gas at STP is
questions.x: 11.2 L = 0.5 mol N₂ molecules; each has 2 atoms, so atoms = 0.5 × 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 6.022 × 10²³.
questions.trap: 3.011 × 10²³ counts molecules, not atoms.

questions.q: Heating 10 g of CaCO₃ should give 4.4 g of CO₂, but only 3.3 g is obtained. The percentage yield is
questions.x: % yield = actual/theoretical × 100 = 3.3/4.4 × 100 = 75%.

questions.q: Phosphate radical is trivalent and calcium is bivalent. The formula of calcium phosphate is
questions.x: Cross the valencies: Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ (total charge 6+ and 6−).

questions.q: A compound has empirical formula CH₂O and molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹. Its molecular formula is
questions.x: Empirical formula mass = 30; n = 180/30 = 6; molecular formula = (CH₂O)₆ = C₆H₁₂O₆.

questions.q: Total number of orbitals in the third shell (n = 3) is
questions.x: Orbitals in shell n = n² = 3² = 9 (one 3s, three 3p, five 3d).
questions.trap: 18 is the maximum number of electrons (2n²).

questions.q: According to the (n + l) rule, the subshell filled immediately after 4s is
questions.x: 4s has n + l = 4; next lowest are 3d (3 + 2 = 5) and 4p (4 + 1 = 5); with equal n + l, lower n (3d) fills first.
questions.trap: 4p: assuming the same shell fills before an inner d subshell.

questions.q: Which subshell has the highest energy in a multi-electron atom?
questions.x: n + l: 4f = 7, 6s = 6, 5p = 6, 5s = 5. Highest n + l means highest energy, so 4f.

questions.q: Rutherford's α-particle scattering experiment showed that
o: electrons move in fixed circular orbits
the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
the atom is a uniform sphere of positive charge
questions.x: Most α-particles passed straight through (atom mostly empty); a few bounced back from a small, dense, positive nucleus.
questions.trap: Fixed orbits is Bohr's postulate, not Rutherford's finding.

questions.q: Energy of the electron in the second Bohr orbit of a hydrogen atom is
questions.trap: −6.8 eV: dividing by n instead of n².

questions.q: The spectral series of hydrogen that lies in the visible region is the
questions.x: Balmer lines end at n = 2 and fall in the visible region; Lyman is UV; Paschen and Brackett are infrared.

questions.q: Maximum number of spectral lines emitted when an electron in hydrogen falls from n = 4 to the ground state is
questions.x: Number of lines = n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6.
questions.trap: 3: counting only direct jumps from each level to ground.

questions.q: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states that it is impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly the
o: mass and charge of an electron
position and momentum of an electron
energy and charge of an electron
spin and mass of an electron
questions.x: Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π; the more precisely position is known, the less precisely momentum is known.

questions.q: In nitrogen (1s² 2s² 2p³) the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins. This follows
questions.x: Hund's rule: pairing in degenerate orbitals starts only after each orbital has one electron with parallel spin.

questions.q: The configuration 1s³ is impossible because it violates
questions.x: An orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins; no two electrons can have all four quantum numbers the same.

questions.q: Number of unpaired electrons in Fe³⁺ (Z of Fe = 26) is
questions.x: Fe = [Ar]3d⁶4s²; Fe³⁺ loses 4s² and one 3d electron → 3d⁵, all five unpaired.
questions.trap: 4: removing all three electrons from 3d instead of 4s first.

questions.q: The tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself is called
questions.x: Electronegativity refers to a bonded atom pulling the shared pair; electron affinity is energy released when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron.
questions.trap: Electron affinity: it concerns isolated atoms, not bonded ones.

questions.q: Which atom has the largest atomic radius?
questions.x: Across period 3 nuclear charge rises while the shell stays the same, so radius decreases: Na > Mg > Al > Si.

questions.q: Which species is the largest?
questions.x: Adding an electron increases repulsion and lowers effective nuclear charge per electron, so Cl⁻ > Cl > Cl⁺; Na⁺ has only two shells.

questions.q: The modern periodic law states that properties of elements are a periodic function of their
questions.x: Moseley showed atomic number is the fundamental property; Mendeleev's law used atomic mass.
questions.trap: Atomic mass: that is Mendeleev's older law.

questions.q: An element has configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵. Its position in the periodic table is
questions.x: Highest n = 4 gives period 4; last electron enters p, and 2 + 5 = 7 valence electrons → group 17 (bromine).
questions.trap: Group 7: counting the 7 valence electrons but ignoring the block.

questions.q: Which set of species is isoelectronic?
questions.x: N³⁻ (7 + 3), O²⁻ (8 + 2) and F⁻ (9 + 1) each have 10 electrons.

questions.q: The second ionisation energy of sodium is much higher than its first because
o: the second electron is removed from 3s
Na⁺ has a stable noble gas (neon) configuration
questions.x: After losing 3s¹, Na⁺ is 1s²2s²2p⁶; the next electron must come from a complete inner shell close to the nucleus.

questions.q: Down a group of the periodic table, metallic character
questions.x: Atomic size increases down a group, so ionisation energy falls and atoms lose electrons more easily.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Molecules of liquid benzene are held together mainly by
questions.x: Benzene is non-polar and has no O–H or N–H bonds, so only weak van der Waals dispersion forces act between its molecules.
questions.trap: Hydrogen bonds: benzene has no H on N, O or F.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Number of σ and π bonds in ethyne (HC≡CH) is
questions.x: Two C–H σ bonds plus one σ in C≡C give 3 σ; the triple bond also has 2 π bonds.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Correct order of bond angle is
questions.x: All sp³; lone pairs repel more: CH₄ 109.5° (0 lp) > NH₃ 107° (1 lp) > H₂O 104.5° (2 lp).

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: A coordinate (dative) covalent bond is present in
questions.x: In NH₄⁺, N donates its lone pair to H⁺, forming a coordinate bond.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethene (C₂H₄) is
questions.x: Each C forms three σ bonds and one π bond; three σ bonds need sp² hybrid orbitals (planar, 120°).

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: The C–C bond length is shortest in
questions.x: Bond length decreases as bond order increases: C≡C (120 pm) < C=C (134 pm) < benzene C–C (139 pm) < C–C (154 pm).

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Ice floats on water because of
o: hydrogen bonding giving an open cage structure
questions.x: Hydrogen bonds hold ice molecules in an open tetrahedral network, so ice is less dense than liquid water.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Shape of ClF₃ according to VSEPR theory is
questions.x: Cl has 3 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs = 5 pairs (sp³d); both lone pairs take equatorial positions, giving a T shape.
questions.trap: Trigonal planar: counting only the 3 bonds.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Metallic bonding is best described as
o: sharing of electron pairs between two atoms
positive metal ions held in a sea of mobile electrons
transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal
questions.x: Valence electrons are delocalised over the lattice of cations; this explains conductivity and malleability.

questions.q: Oxidation number of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇ is
questions.trap: +12: forgetting to divide by the two Cr atoms.

questions.q: Oxidation number of Cl in HClO₄ is
questions.trap: +5 is Cl in chlorate (ClO₃⁻).

questions.q: Oxidation number of oxygen in OF₂ is
questions.x: F is more electronegative and is always −1: x + 2(−1) = 0 → x = +2.
questions.trap: −2: applying the usual rule for oxygen blindly.

questions.q: According to the classical concept, reduction is
o: removal of oxygen or addition of hydrogen
questions.x: Classically, oxidation = addition of O / removal of H; reduction is the reverse (e.g. CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O reduces CuO).
questions.trap: Loss of electrons is oxidation in the electronic concept.

questions.q: In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, the oxidising agent is
questions.x: Cu²⁺ gains electrons (is reduced) and so oxidises Zn; Zn is the reducing agent.
questions.trap: Zn: it is oxidised, which makes it the reducing agent.

questions.q: In acidic medium, one mole of MnO₄⁻ oxidises how many moles of Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺?
questions.x: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O; each Fe²⁺ gives 1 e⁻, so 5 Fe²⁺ per MnO₄⁻.

questions.q: When Cl₂ reacts with cold dilute NaOH to give NaCl and NaOCl, chlorine is
questions.x: Cl goes from 0 to −1 in NaCl (reduced) and 0 to +1 in NaOCl (oxidised): a disproportionation reaction.

questions.q: Under the same conditions, the ratio of rates of diffusion of helium to methane is
questions.trap: 4 : 1: forgetting the square root.

questions.q: An open flask contains air at 27 °C. It is heated to 327 °C at the same pressure. The fraction of air that escapes is
questions.x: Same P and V: n ∝ 1/T. n₂/n₁ = 300/600 = 1/2, so half the air remains and half escapes.
questions.trap: Using °C: 27/327 gives a wrong ratio; always use kelvin.

questions.q: At constant temperature, if the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is doubled, its volume becomes
questions.x: Boyle's law: PV = constant at constant T, so doubling P halves V.

questions.q: A gas at 0 °C is heated to 273 °C at constant pressure. Its volume becomes
questions.x: Charles' law: V ∝ T(K). 0 °C = 273 K, 273 °C = 546 K; ratio 546/273 = 2.

questions.q: Value of the gas constant R in L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is
questions.x: R = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 1.987 cal K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
questions.trap: 8.314 is the value in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: A real gas behaves most nearly like an ideal gas at
questions.x: At low P molecules are far apart (own volume negligible); at high T attractions are overcome by kinetic energy.

questions.q: In the van der Waals equation, the constant 'a' corrects for
questions.x: 'a' corrects pressure for attractions (P + an²/V²); 'b' corrects for the finite volume of molecules.
questions.trap: Volume of molecules is corrected by 'b'.

questions.q: A mixture of 1 mol O₂ and 3 mol N₂ has a total pressure of 8 atm. The partial pressure of O₂ is
questions.x: Dalton's law: p(O₂) = mole fraction × P = (1/4) × 8 = 2 atm.

questions.q: When the absolute temperature of a gas is raised from 300 K to 1200 K, its rms speed becomes
questions.trap: Four times: forgetting the square root.

questions.q: When the temperature of a liquid is raised, its surface tension
questions.x: Higher kinetic energy weakens intermolecular attraction at the surface, so surface tension falls (zero at the critical temperature).

questions.q: Water boils below 100 °C at the top of a high mountain because
o: the vapour pressure of water is higher there
the atmospheric pressure is lower there
questions.x: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure; lower outside pressure is reached at a lower temperature.

questions.q: Viscosity of a liquid on increasing temperature
questions.x: Heating weakens intermolecular forces in a liquid, so it flows more easily (e.g. hot honey).
questions.trap: Increases: that is true for gases, not liquids.

questions.q: A liquid boils at the temperature at which its vapour pressure
questions.x: At the boiling point, bubbles of vapour can form throughout the liquid because vapour pressure matches the pressure above it.

questions.q: A liquid crystal is
o: an ionic solid dissolved in water
a state intermediate between crystalline solid and liquid
a crystal containing water of crystallisation
questions.x: Liquid crystals flow like liquids but keep some molecular order like crystals; they are used in LCD displays.

questions.q: Number of atoms per unit cell in a face-centred cubic (fcc) lattice is
questions.x: 8 corners × 1/8 = 1, plus 6 faces × 1/2 = 3; total = 4.
questions.trap: 2 is for body-centred cubic.

questions.q: Number of atoms per unit cell in a body-centred cubic (bcc) lattice is
questions.x: 8 corners × 1/8 = 1, plus 1 atom at the body centre = 2.
questions.trap: 9: counting every atom as fully inside the cell.

questions.q: Total number of Bravais lattices is
questions.x: The 7 crystal systems give 14 Bravais lattices.
questions.trap: 7 is the number of crystal systems.

questions.q: Unit cell parameters a = b = c and α = β = γ = 90° belong to the
questions.x: Cubic: all edges equal, all angles 90°. Tetragonal has a = b ≠ c; rhombohedral has equal edges but angles ≠ 90°.

questions.q: Washing soda crystals (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) lose water of crystallisation on exposure to air and become powdery. This is called
questions.x: Efflorescent salts give up water to the air; deliquescent substances absorb moisture and dissolve.
questions.trap: Deliquescence is the opposite: absorbing moisture.

questions.q: Which substance is deliquescent?
questions.x: Solid NaOH absorbs so much moisture from air that it dissolves in it; washing soda is efflorescent.

questions.q: Which is a covalent (network) crystal?
questions.x: In diamond each C is covalently bonded to four others in a 3-D network; NaCl is ionic, ice molecular, Cu metallic.

questions.q: Glass is an amorphous solid because it
o: has no long-range order and no sharp melting point
questions.x: Amorphous solids have short-range order only; they soften over a range of temperature and are isotropic.

questions.q: Number of molecules of water of crystallisation in blue vitriol is
questions.x: Blue vitriol is CuSO₄·5H₂O. (7: green/white vitriol; 10: washing soda.)

questions.q: Increasing the pressure shifts which equilibrium in the forward direction?
questions.x: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles: 4 → 2 for NH₃. H₂ + I₂ has no change (2 → 2); the others increase gas moles.

questions.q: For the endothermic reaction N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), raising the temperature
o: shifts equilibrium backward and decreases K
shifts equilibrium forward and increases K
changes the rate but not K
questions.x: Heat favours the endothermic (forward) direction, so K rises. Δn = 0 only removes the pressure effect, not the temperature effect.
questions.trap: No effect: confusing the pressure rule (Δn = 0) with temperature.

questions.q: Adding a catalyst to a system at equilibrium
o: makes no change in the equilibrium composition
questions.x: A catalyst speeds forward and backward reactions equally; equilibrium is reached faster but K is unchanged.

questions.q: For A ⇌ B, K = 4. The equilibrium constant for 2B ⇌ 2A is
questions.x: Reversing gives 1/K = 1/4; doubling the coefficients squares it: (1/4)² = 1/16.
questions.trap: 1/8: halving instead of squaring.

questions.q: If the reaction quotient Q is less than the equilibrium constant K, the reaction
questions.x: Q < K means too few products; the reaction moves forward until Q = K.

questions.q: Unit of Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is
questions.x: Kc = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³) has (mol L⁻¹)^(2 − 4) = (mol L⁻¹)⁻² = L² mol⁻².

questions.q: A 500 g sample of water contains 0.01 g of Ca²⁺ ions. Concentration of Ca²⁺ in ppm is
questions.x: ppm = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 10⁶ = (0.01/500) × 10⁶ = 20 ppm.

questions.q: Volume of 0.02 M KMnO₄ needed to oxidise 25 mL of 0.1 M oxalic acid in acidic medium is
questions.x: 2MnO₄⁻ ≡ 5C₂O₄²⁻. Oxalic acid = 2.5 mmol → MnO₄⁻ = 2.5 × 2/5 = 1 mmol; V = 1/0.02 = 50 mL.
questions.trap: 125 mL: using the 5 : 2 ratio upside down.

questions.q: 4 g of NaOH is dissolved in 500 g of water. The molality of the solution is
questions.x: Moles = 4/40 = 0.1; molality = 0.1 mol / 0.5 kg solvent = 0.2 mol kg⁻¹.

questions.q: A solution contains 1 mol of glucose and 9 mol of water. Mole fraction of glucose is
questions.trap: 1/9: dividing by moles of water instead of total moles.

questions.q: Normality of 0.5 M H₂SO₄ is
questions.x: H₂SO₄ is dibasic (n-factor 2): N = M × 2 = 1 N.

questions.q: Which can be used as a primary standard substance?
questions.x: A primary standard is pure, stable and non-hygroscopic. NaOH absorbs moisture and CO₂; KMnO₄ decomposes; conc. HCl is volatile.
questions.trap: NaOH: common lab base, but it is hygroscopic.

questions.q: Mass of oxalic acid crystals (H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O, M = 126) needed to make 250 mL of 0.1 N solution is
questions.x: Equivalent weight = 126/2 = 63. Equivalents = 0.1 × 0.25 = 0.025; mass = 0.025 × 63 = 1.575 g.
questions.trap: 3.15 g: using molar mass 126 instead of equivalent weight.

questions.q: Molarity of a 10% (w/v) NaOH solution is
Solubility of AgCl is least in
questions.x: The common ion Cl⁻ from NaCl pushes AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ back. NH₃ dissolves AgCl by forming [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺.
questions.trap: 0.1 M NH₃: it actually increases solubility via a complex.

questions.q: According to Ostwald's dilution law, on diluting a weak electrolyte its degree of ionisation
questions.x: α = √(Ka/C); lowering C increases α.

questions.q: pH of 10⁻⁸ M HCl solution is about
questions.x: Water's own 10⁻⁷ M H⁺ cannot be ignored: [H⁺] ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ M, pH ≈ 6.98 (slightly acidic).
questions.trap: 8: an acid solution can never have pH above 7.

questions.q: pH of 0.001 M HCl is
questions.x: HCl is fully ionised: [H⁺] = 10⁻³ M, pH = −log 10⁻³ = 3.

questions.q: Conjugate base of H₂O is
questions.x: Removing one H⁺ from H₂O gives OH⁻; adding H⁺ gives its conjugate acid H₃O⁺.
questions.trap: H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid.

questions.q: Aqueous solution of which salt is acidic?
questions.x: NH₄Cl is a salt of a strong acid and weak base; NH₄⁺ hydrolyses to give H₃O⁺. CH₃COONa and Na₂CO₃ are basic; NaCl neutral.

questions.q: Ksp of AgCl is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰. Its solubility in water is about
questions.trap: 4 × 10⁻⁵: √16 = 4, but the exponent −10 makes it √1.6 × 10⁻⁵.

questions.q: A precipitate forms when the ionic product of a sparingly soluble salt
questions.x: Ionic product > Ksp: solution is supersaturated and the salt precipitates; < Ksp: more salt can dissolve.

questions.q: A buffer contains equal concentrations of acetic acid (pKa = 4.74) and sodium acetate. Its pH is
questions.x: Henderson equation: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.74 + log 1 = 4.74.

questions.q: A stronger acid has
questions.x: pKa = −log Ka; larger Ka (stronger acid) gives smaller pKa.

questions.q: For a reaction with rate = k[A]²[B]^½, the overall order is
questions.x: Overall order = sum of powers in the rate law = 2 + ½ = 2.5.

questions.q: For A → products, doubling [A] makes the rate four times. The order with respect to A is
questions.x: Rate ∝ [A]ⁿ: 2ⁿ = 4 → n = 2.
questions.trap: 4: equating order to the rate factor.

questions.q: A reaction has rate constant k = 2.0 × 10⁻³ L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. Its order is
questions.x: Unit of k = (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) s⁻¹; L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ means 1 − n = −1, so n = 2.

questions.q: Which statement about order and molecularity is correct?
o: Order and molecularity are always equal
Molecularity is found by experiment and can be zero
Order can be written directly from the balanced equation
Order is found by experiment and can be fractional; molecularity is always a whole number
questions.x: Order comes from the experimental rate law (0, fractional allowed); molecularity counts molecules in an elementary step (1, 2, 3).
questions.trap: Writing order from the balanced equation works only for elementary steps.

questions.q: For a zero-order reaction, the half-life is
o: directly proportional to the initial concentration
inversely proportional to the initial concentration
questions.x: Zero order: t½ = [A]₀/2k, so it increases with [A]₀. 0.693/k is for first order.
questions.trap: 0.693/k is the first-order formula.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has k = 0.0693 min⁻¹. Its half-life is
Time taken for 99.9% completion of a first-order reaction is about
questions.x: Fraction left 1/1000 ≈ (½)¹⁰ = 1/1024; n = log 1000/log 2 ≈ 10.

questions.q: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by
questions.x: A catalyst provides an alternative path with lower Eₐ, so more molecules have enough energy to react.

questions.q: According to collision theory, a collision is effective only when molecules
o: have energy at least equal to the threshold energy and proper orientation
questions.x: Effective collisions need both enough energy (≥ threshold) and correct orientation to form the activated complex.

questions.q: For most reactions, a 10 °C rise in temperature makes the rate about
questions.x: The temperature coefficient (k at T + 10 / k at T) is usually 2 to 3.

questions.q: Which is an example of heterogeneous catalysis?
o: SO₂ oxidised by O₂ with NO gas (lead chamber)
hydrolysis of ester with dilute acid
decomposition of H₂O₂ by aqueous I⁻
questions.x: In the Haber process the catalyst (solid Fe) is in a different phase from the gaseous reactants.

questions.q: In a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with alkaline electrolyte, the reaction at the anode is
questions.x: Oxidation occurs at the anode: H₂ is oxidised. O₂ is reduced at the cathode. Overall 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
questions.trap: O₂ reduction: that is the cathode reaction.

questions.q: The standard hydrogen electrode has an electrode potential of
questions.x: SHE (Pt, H₂ at 1 atm, 1 M H⁺) is the reference electrode, assigned zero potential at all temperatures.

questions.q: The strongest reducing agent among the following is
questions.x: Li has the most negative standard reduction potential (−3.04 V), so it loses electrons most readily.

questions.q: A current of 2 A is passed through CuSO₄ solution for 965 s. Mass of copper deposited is (Cu = 63.5)
questions.trap: 1.27 g: forgetting Cu²⁺ needs 2 electrons.

questions.q: Which is a secondary (rechargeable) cell?
questions.x: In the lead storage battery the cell reaction can be reversed by charging; the others are primary cells.

questions.q: The calomel electrode contains
questions.x: Calomel is mercurous chloride, Hg₂Cl₂, in contact with Hg and KCl solution. HgCl₂ is corrosive sublimate.
questions.trap: HgCl₂ is corrosive sublimate, not calomel.

questions.q: On electrolysis of concentrated aqueous NaCl, the products at cathode and anode are
o: Na at cathode, Cl₂ at anode
H₂ at cathode, Cl₂ at anode
H₂ at cathode, O₂ at anode
Na at cathode, O₂ at anode
questions.x: Water is reduced more easily than Na⁺, giving H₂; in concentrated brine Cl⁻ is oxidised to Cl₂ (NaOH remains).
questions.trap: Na at cathode happens only for molten NaCl.

questions.q: Copper sulphate solution cannot be stored in a vessel made of
questions.x: Zn is above Cu in the electrochemical series and displaces it: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.

questions.q: When the same charge passes through different electrolytes, masses of substances liberated are proportional to their
questions.x: Faraday's second law: w₁/w₂ = E₁/E₂, where E is the equivalent weight.

questions.q: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of
questions.x: Energy can be converted from one form to another but the total energy of system and surroundings is constant: ΔU = q + w.
questions.trap: Increase of entropy is the second law.

questions.q: A system absorbs 50 J of heat and 20 J of work is done on it. Change in its internal energy is
questions.x: Heat in and work done on the system both add energy: ΔU = q + w = 50 + 20 = +70 J.
questions.trap: +30 J: treating work done on the system as negative.

questions.q: A sealed, perfectly insulated thermos flask containing tea is an example of
questions.x: An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings.

questions.q: Which is a state function?
questions.x: State functions depend only on initial and final states (U, H, S, G); heat and work depend on the path.

questions.q: Which is an intensive property?
questions.x: Intensive properties do not depend on amount of substance (temperature, density, pressure); mass, volume and enthalpy are extensive.

questions.q: Given C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ and CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283 kJ. ΔH for C + ½O₂ → CO is
questions.x: Hess's law: subtract the second equation from the first: −393.5 − (−283) = −110.5 kJ.

questions.q: Enthalpy of neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base is about −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹. For acetic acid with NaOH it is
questions.x: Some heat is used to ionise the weak acid, so less heat is released (about −55 kJ mol⁻¹).

questions.q: Entropy of the system increases when
questions.x: Melting changes an ordered solid into a more disordered liquid; the others increase order.

questions.q: For a reaction at equilibrium with K > 1, the standard free energy change ΔG° is
questions.x: ΔG° = −2.303RT log K; if K > 1, log K > 0, so ΔG° < 0.
questions.trap: Zero: ΔG (not ΔG°) is zero at equilibrium.

questions.q: A reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures when
o: ΔH is positive and ΔS is negative
ΔH is negative and ΔS is positive
ΔH and ΔS are both positive
ΔH and ΔS are both negative
questions.x: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is then negative at every temperature.

questions.q: Enthalpy of formation of HCl is −92 kJ mol⁻¹. By Laplace's law, enthalpy of decomposition of HCl into its elements is
questions.x: Laplace's law: ΔH of decomposition is equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to ΔH of formation.

questions.q: Complete the reaction: ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + ?
questions.x: Mass: 14 + 4 = 17 + 1; charge: 7 + 2 = 8 + 1. The particle is ¹₁H, a proton (Rutherford, 1919).

questions.q: Complete the reaction: ⁹₄Be + ⁴₂He → ¹²₆C + ?
questions.x: Mass: 9 + 4 = 12 + 1; charge: 4 + 2 = 6 + 0. The particle is a neutron (Chadwick's discovery).

questions.q: Emission of a γ-ray from a nucleus
o: changes neither atomic number nor mass number
questions.x: γ-rays are high-energy photons with no mass or charge; they only remove excess energy.

questions.q: ²³⁸₉₂U emits one α-particle and then two β-particles. The final nucleus is
questions.x: α: A − 4, Z − 2 → ²³⁴₉₀Th. Two β: Z + 2 → ²³⁴₉₂U, an isotope of the parent.
questions.trap: ²³⁴₉₀Th: stopping after the α step.

questions.q: Half-life of C-14 is 5730 years. Fraction of C-14 left in a wooden object 11460 years old is
questions.x: 11460/5730 = 2 half-lives; fraction left = (½)² = 1/4.

questions.q: A radioisotope has half-life 2 days. From 16 g, the mass left after 6 days is
questions.x: 6 days = 3 half-lives: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 g.

questions.q: The energy of the Sun is produced mainly by
o: nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
questions.x: In the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, converting mass into energy (E = mc²).

questions.q: Lassaigne's (sodium fusion) extract is prepared to detect
o: functional groups of an organic compound
nitrogen, sulphur and halogens in an organic compound
questions.x: Fusing with Na converts covalently bound N, S and X into ionic NaCN, Na₂S and NaX, which give ordinary ionic tests.

questions.q: In Lassaigne's test, nitrogen is confirmed by the formation of
questions.x: NaCN + FeSO₄ → Na₄[Fe(CN)₆]; with Fe³⁺ it gives Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃, Prussian blue.
questions.trap: Violet with nitroprusside is the test for sulphur.

questions.q: In Lassaigne's extract, sulphur gives a violet colour with
questions.x: Na₂S + Na₂[Fe(CN)₅NO] → violet Na₄[Fe(CN)₅NOS]. (S also gives a black PbS ppt with lead acetate.)

questions.q: Baeyer's reagent is
questions.x: Alkenes and alkynes decolourise the pink colour of cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ (forming a brown MnO₂ ppt).
questions.trap: Ammoniacal AgNO₃ is Tollens' reagent.

questions.q: Decolourisation of bromine water by an organic compound indicates
questions.x: Br₂ adds across multiple bonds, so its reddish-brown colour disappears.

questions.q: A red precipitate with ammoniacal cuprous chloride is given by
questions.x: Terminal alkynes have acidic ≡C–H; ethyne forms red copper acetylide. Ethene has no such H.

questions.q: Ethene and ethyne can be distinguished by
o: ammoniacal AgNO₃ (white precipitate with ethyne only)
questions.x: Both decolourise bromine water and Baeyer's reagent; only the terminal alkyne gives silver acetylide.
questions.trap: Bromine water: both are unsaturated and both decolourise it.

questions.q: Hydrogen sulphide gas turns lead acetate paper
questions.x: Pb(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂S → PbS (black) + 2CH₃COOH.

questions.q: Colour of methyl orange in an alkaline solution is
questions.x: Methyl orange is red below pH 3.1 and yellow above 4.4.
questions.trap: Pink is phenolphthalein in base.

questions.q: Suitable indicator for titrating acetic acid with NaOH is
questions.x: Weak acid–strong base: end point pH is above 7 (about 8–9), matching phenolphthalein's range 8.3–10.
questions.trap: Methyl orange changes colour too early, in acidic range.

questions.q: Suitable indicator for titrating HCl with NH₄OH is
questions.x: Strong acid–weak base: end point is acidic (pH about 5), within methyl orange's range.
questions.trap: Phenolphthalein suits weak acid vs strong base.

questions.q: For the titration of acetic acid with ammonium hydroxide
o: no simple indicator gives a sharp end point
questions.x: Weak acid vs weak base gives no steep pH jump at equivalence, so colour change is not sharp.

questions.q: In the Victor Meyer test, a primary alcohol gives
questions.x: 1° alcohol → nitrolic acid → blood red; 2° → pseudonitrole → blue; 3° → colourless.
questions.trap: Blue is the result for a secondary alcohol.

questions.q: Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with
questions.x: Aldehydes reduce ammoniacal AgNO₃ to metallic silver; ketones like acetone do not.

questions.q: Which compound does NOT reduce Fehling's solution?
questions.x: Aromatic aldehydes give Tollens' test but not Fehling's; aliphatic aldehydes and glucose give a red Cu₂O ppt.

questions.q: Ethanol and methanol can be distinguished by
questions.x: Ethanol has CH₃CH(OH)– and gives yellow CHI₃ with I₂/NaOH; methanol does not. Both react with Na.

questions.q: In the Lucas test, immediate turbidity at room temperature is given by
questions.x: Lucas reagent (conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl₂) forms insoluble alkyl chloride fastest with 3° alcohols (stable carbocation).

questions.q: A violet colour in the biuret test indicates
questions.x: Peptide bonds form a violet complex with Cu²⁺ in alkaline CuSO₄.

questions.q: Starch is detected by
o: a blue-black colour with iodine solution
a violet colour with biuret reagent
a red colour with Sudan III
a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent
questions.x: Iodine fits inside the amylose helix, giving the blue-black colour.

questions.q: A white precipitate with AgNO₃ that dissolves in NH₄OH shows the presence of
questions.x: AgCl is white and soluble in ammonia; AgBr is pale yellow (partly soluble), AgI yellow (insoluble).

questions.q: A white precipitate with BaCl₂ solution, insoluble in dilute HCl, confirms
questions.x: BaSO₄ is insoluble in acids; BaCO₃ would dissolve in HCl with effervescence.
questions.trap: Carbonate: BaCO₃ dissolves in HCl.

questions.q: Nessler's reagent gives a brown precipitate with
questions.x: Nessler's reagent (alkaline K₂HgI₄) gives a brown ppt (iodide of Millon's base) with ammonia/NH₄⁺.

questions.q: Brick-red colour in the flame test indicates
questions.x: Ca: brick red; Na: golden yellow; K: lilac; Ba: apple green.

questions.q: A mixture of common salt and camphor can be separated by
questions.x: Camphor sublimes on heating and collects on a cool surface; NaCl does not sublime.

questions.q: Glycerol, which decomposes at its normal boiling point, is purified by
questions.x: Lowering the pressure lowers the boiling point, so the liquid distils below its decomposition temperature.

questions.q: Two miscible liquids with close boiling points are separated by
questions.x: A fractionating column gives repeated vaporisation–condensation, separating liquids whose boiling points differ only slightly.

questions.q: In paper chromatography, the Rf value of a substance is
o: distance moved by the substance ÷ distance moved by the solvent front
distance moved by the solvent ÷ distance moved by the substance
the time taken by the solvent to rise
questions.x: Rf = distance travelled by solute / distance travelled by solvent front, so 0 < Rf < 1.

questions.q: Atmolysis is the separation of
o: gases by their different rates of diffusion
questions.x: Atmolysis uses Graham's law: lighter gases diffuse faster through a porous partition.

questions.q: Fractional crystallisation separates substances that differ in their
questions.x: The less soluble component crystallises first on cooling or concentrating the solution.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes iodometry from iodimetry?
o: Iodometry uses KMnO₄ as indicator; iodimetry uses starch
Iodimetry titrates liberated I₂ with hypo; iodometry uses standard I₂ directly
In iodometry, I₂ liberated by an oxidant is titrated with hypo; in iodimetry, a standard I₂ solution is used directly
questions.x: Iodometric: oxidant + excess KI → I₂, titrated with Na₂S₂O₃. Iodimetric: reducing agent titrated directly with I₂. Starch is the indicator in both.
questions.trap: Swapping the two names is the common error.

questions.q: In permanganometric titrations no external indicator is needed because
o: KMnO₄ acts as its own (self) indicator
the solution is colourless at the end
questions.x: Purple MnO₄⁻ becomes colourless Mn²⁺; the first excess drop gives a permanent pink colour.

questions.q: Hardness of water is estimated by complexometric titration with
questions.x: EDTA forms stable 1 : 1 complexes with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺; EBT changes from wine red to blue at the end point.

questions.q: The vapour density of a gas is 32. Its molar mass is
questions.x: Molar mass = 2 × vapour density = 2 × 32 = 64 g mol⁻¹ (e.g. SO₂).
questions.trap: 32: forgetting the factor of 2 (VD is relative to H₂, M = 2).

questions.q: An ion X²⁺ has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 8. If the mass number of X is 40, the number of neutrons in its nucleus is
questions.x: X²⁺ has 18 electrons, so neutral X has 20 electrons and Z = 20. Neutrons = A − Z = 40 − 20 = 20.
questions.trap: 22: taking Z as the ion's electron count (18).

questions.q: Which substance can act both as an oxidising agent and as a reducing agent?
questions.x: O in H₂O₂ is −1, between 0 and −2, so it can be oxidised or reduced (like N +3 in HNO₂, S +4 in SO₂). HNO₃ and KMnO₄ are in highest states; S in H₂S is lowest.

questions.q: In acidic medium, how many moles of H₂S are oxidised to sulphur by 2 moles of KMnO₄?
questions.x: MnO₄⁻ gains 5 e⁻; H₂S → S loses 2 e⁻. 2 mol KMnO₄ take 10 e⁻ = 5 mol H₂S. (2MnO₄⁻ + 5H₂S + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5S + 8H₂O)
questions.trap: 2.5: that is per mole of KMnO₄, not per 2 moles.

questions.q: Commercial sulphuric acid is 98% H₂SO₄ by mass with density 1.84 g mL⁻¹. Its molarity is about
questions.trap: 36.8 M is the normality (n-factor 2), not molarity.

questions.q: In the reaction HF + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + F⁻, the two Brønsted acids are
questions.x: A Brønsted acid donates H⁺: HF forward, H₃O⁺ in reverse. F⁻ and H₂O are the bases (conjugate pairs HF/F⁻ and H₃O⁺/H₂O).
questions.trap: HF and F⁻ is a conjugate pair: one acid, one base.

questions.q: Iron pipes buried in soil are protected by connecting them to a block of magnesium. Here magnesium acts as
questions.x: Mg has a more negative E° than Fe, so Mg is oxidised (anode) instead of iron: cathodic protection. Zinc in galvanising works the same way.

questions.q: Before testing Lassaigne's extract for halogens with AgNO₃, it is boiled with dilute HNO₃ in order to
o: make the silver halide more soluble
decompose NaCN and Na₂S, which would otherwise interfere
convert halide ions into free halogens
remove the excess sodium metal as NaNO₃
questions.x: CN⁻ and S²⁻ would give AgCN (white) and Ag₂S (black) with AgNO₃; boiling with HNO₃ expels them as HCN and H₂S.

questions.q: Benedict's solution gives a red precipitate of Cu₂O with
questions.x: Benedict's (Cu²⁺ citrate) is reduced by aliphatic aldehydes and reducing sugars. Sucrose is non-reducing; ketones and aromatic aldehydes do not reduce it.
questions.trap: Benzaldehyde: aromatic aldehydes reduce Tollens' but not Benedict's/Fehling's.

questions.q: Number of significant figures in 0.00450 is
questions.x: Leading zeros only locate the decimal point and are not significant; the trailing zero after the decimal point is. Significant digits: 4, 5, 0.
questions.trap: 5 or 6: counting the leading zeros.

questions.q: Percentage of water of crystallisation in blue vitriol, CuSO₄·5H₂O (M = 249.5), is about
questions.trap: 56.4%: dividing by the anhydrous mass 159.5 instead of 249.5.

questions.q: Avogadro's number is equal to the number of
o: molecules in 1 g of hydrogen gas
atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12
molecules in 22.4 L of a gas at 25 °C and 1 atm
electrons that carry a charge of 1 coulomb
questions.x: One mole is the amount containing as many entities as there are atoms in 12 g of C-12, i.e. 6.022 × 10²³.
questions.trap: 1 g of H₂ is only 0.5 mol of molecules.

questions.q: 1 L of a gas at STP weighs 1.25 g. Its vapour density is
questions.x: Molar mass = 1.25 × 22.4 = 28 g mol⁻¹. Vapour density = M/2 = 14.
questions.trap: 28: stopping at molar mass and forgetting VD = M/2.

questions.q: A hydrocarbon contains 80% carbon and 20% hydrogen by mass. Its empirical formula is
questions.x: Mole ratio C : H = 80/12 : 20/1 = 6.67 : 20 = 1 : 3, so CH₃ (molecular formula could be C₂H₆).
questions.trap: CH₄: guessing the simplest hydrocarbon instead of computing the ratio.

questions.q: Mass of one mole of electrons (mass of an electron = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) is about
questions.trap: 1.008 g is the mass of a mole of hydrogen atoms, not electrons.

questions.q: 0.9 g of a metal displaces 1.12 L of H₂ at STP from an acid. The equivalent mass of the metal is
questions.x: 11.2 L H₂ at STP = 1 g H = 1 equivalent. 1.12 L = 0.1 equivalent, so equivalent mass = 0.9/0.1 = 9 (the metal is aluminium).
questions.trap: 18: using 22.4 L as one equivalent of hydrogen.

questions.q: 5.6 L of a gas at STP weighs 11 g. Its molar mass is
The law of conservation of mass was established by
questions.x: Lavoisier showed that the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products in a chemical change.

questions.q: Volume of oxygen needed for complete combustion of 10 mL of methane, all volumes at the same T and P, is
questions.x: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. By Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes, 10 mL CH₄ needs 2 × 10 = 20 mL O₂.

questions.q: 3 mol of H₂ and 2 mol of O₂ are allowed to react to form water. The limiting reagent and the moles of water formed are
questions.x: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 3 mol H₂ needs only 1.5 mol O₂, so H₂ runs out first; water = 3 mol (0.5 mol O₂ left).
questions.trap: O₂; 4 mol: taking water from O₂ without checking which reactant runs out.

questions.q: 28 g of N₂ and 9 g of H₂ react to form ammonia (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃). The maximum mass of NH₃ formed is
questions.x: N₂ = 1 mol needs 3 mol (6 g) H₂; 4.5 mol H₂ is present, so N₂ is limiting. NH₃ = 2 mol × 17 = 34 g.
questions.trap: 51 g: using H₂ (4.5 mol) as the limiting reagent.

questions.q: Which sample contains the largest number of atoms?
questions.x: Moles of atoms: H₂ 1/2 × 2 = 1; He 1/4 = 0.25; O₂ 1/32 × 2 = 0.0625; CH₄ 1/16 × 5 = 0.31. H₂ has the most.

questions.q: Volume of CO₂ at STP obtained when 10 g of CaCO₃ reacts completely with excess dilute HCl is
questions.x: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. 10 g CaCO₃ = 0.1 mol → 0.1 mol CO₂ = 0.1 × 22.4 = 2.24 L.

questions.q: The law of reciprocal proportions was put forward by
questions.x: Richter (1792) stated the law of reciprocal proportions; Proust gave constant proportions and Dalton gave multiple proportions.

questions.q: Ratio of the number of molecules in equal masses of O₂ and SO₂ is
questions.x: Molecules ∝ mass/M. O₂ : SO₂ = (m/32) : (m/64) = 2 : 1.
questions.trap: 1 : 2: putting molar masses in the ratio directly.

questions.q: Maximum number of electrons that the shell with n = 4 can hold is
questions.x: A shell holds n² orbitals and 2n² electrons: 2 × 4² = 32.
questions.trap: 16: that is the number of orbitals (n²), not electrons.

questions.q: According to the Aufbau principle, the subshell filled immediately after 4p is
questions.x: (n + l) for 4p = 5 and 5s = 5; with equal (n + l) the lower n fills first, so 4p then 5s. 4d has n + l = 6.
questions.trap: 4d: assuming all of shell 4 fills before shell 5.

questions.q: Number of neutrons in the ion ³⁷₁₇Cl⁻ is
questions.x: Neutrons = A − Z = 37 − 17 = 20. The extra electron changes only the electron count (18).
questions.trap: 18: counting electrons in the ion instead of neutrons.

questions.q: Number of orbitals in an f subshell is
questions.x: l = 3 for f, so m = −3 … +3, giving 2l + 1 = 7 orbitals (holding 14 electrons).
questions.trap: 14: the number of electrons, not orbitals.

questions.q: Ratio of the radii of the first and second Bohr orbits of the hydrogen atom is
questions.x: Bohr radius r ∝ n²/Z, so r₁ : r₂ = 1² : 2² = 1 : 4.
questions.trap: 1 : 2: taking r proportional to n instead of n².

questions.q: Ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV. The ionisation energy of He⁺ (Z = 2) from its ground state is
questions.x: For a one-electron species E = 13.6 Z²/n² eV. He⁺: 13.6 × 4 = 54.4 eV.
questions.trap: 27.2 eV: multiplying by Z instead of Z².

questions.q: Isotopes of an element differ in the number of
questions.x: Isotopes have the same atomic number (protons) but different mass numbers because their neutron counts differ.

questions.q: The most electronegative element in the periodic table is
questions.x: Fluorine has the highest Pauling electronegativity (4.0): small atom with high effective nuclear charge.
questions.trap: Chlorine: it has the most negative electron gain enthalpy, not the highest electronegativity.

questions.q: Among the isoelectronic ions K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻ and S²⁻, the largest is
questions.x: All have 18 electrons. The ion with the fewest protons (S²⁻, Z = 16) holds its electrons least tightly, so it is largest.
questions.trap: K⁺: thinking a heavier atom always gives a bigger ion.

questions.q: The first ionisation enthalpy of nitrogen is higher than that of oxygen because
o: nitrogen has a stable, half-filled 2p³ configuration
oxygen has a smaller nuclear charge than nitrogen
the oxygen atom is larger than the nitrogen atom
nitrogen has a completely filled 2p subshell
questions.x: Removing an electron from the extra-stable half-filled 2p³ of N costs more energy; O (2p⁴) loses a paired electron more easily.

questions.q: Which element is a metalloid?
questions.x: Metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) show properties between metals and non-metals. Al is a metal; P and S are non-metals.

questions.q: The electron gain enthalpy of fluorine is less negative than that of chlorine because
o: fluorine is less electronegative than chlorine
fluorine has a larger atomic radius than chlorine
the small size of F causes strong repulsion between the added electron and its compact 2p electrons
questions.x: The added electron enters the crowded, small 2p shell of F and is repelled; Cl's larger 3p shell accommodates it more easily.

questions.q: The element in period 4 and group 13 of the periodic table has atomic number
questions.x: Period 4: K(19), Ca(20), then 3d series Sc–Zn (21–30); group 13 follows as Ga, Z = 31.
questions.trap: 21: forgetting the ten d-block elements between groups 2 and 13.

questions.q: A diagonal relationship is shown by
questions.x: Diagonal pairs are Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si (similar charge/size ratio). The other pairs are in the same group.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Shape of the ammonia molecule is
questions.x: N has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair (sp³). The electron pairs are tetrahedral, but the molecular shape is pyramidal.
questions.trap: Tetrahedral: that is the electron-pair geometry, not the shape of the atoms.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Hybridisation of phosphorus in PCl₅ and the shape of the molecule are
questions.x: P has 5 bond pairs and no lone pair: five hybrid orbitals (sp³d) pointing to the corners of a trigonal bipyramid.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Bond order of the N₂ molecule is
questions.x: Bond order = (bonding − antibonding)/2 = (10 − 4)/2 = 3, matching the N≡N triple bond.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Which molecule is linear?
questions.x: C in CO₂ is sp hybridised with no lone pair, giving 180°. H₂O, SO₂ and O₃ are bent because of lone pairs.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Number of lone pairs on xenon in XeF₂ and the shape of the molecule are
questions.x: Xe has 8 valence electrons: 2 bond pairs + 3 lone pairs (sp³d). The lone pairs sit in the equatorial plane, so F–Xe–F is linear.
questions.trap: Bent: assuming lone pairs always bend the molecule, as in water.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: Argon can be liquefied only at a very low temperature because its atoms are held together only by
questions.x: Argon atoms are non-polar; only weak, temporary-dipole (van der Waals) dispersion forces act between them.

questions.s: Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules
questions.q: o-Nitrophenol is more volatile (steam volatile) than p-nitrophenol because
o: p-nitrophenol has a smaller molar mass
questions.x: In the ortho isomer, –OH bonds to the neighbouring –NO₂ within the molecule, so molecules do not associate; the para isomer associates through intermolecular H-bonds.

questions.q: Average oxidation number of sulphur in sodium thiosulphate, Na₂S₂O₃, is
Oxidation number of chlorine in sodium chlorate, NaClO₃, is
questions.x: +1 + x + 3(−2) = 0 → x = +5. (+7 is chlorine in perchlorate, ClO₄⁻.)
questions.trap: +7: mixing up chlorate (ClO₃⁻) with perchlorate (ClO₄⁻).

questions.q: Oxidation number of iron in Fe₃O₄ is
questions.x: 3x + 4(−2) = 0 → x = +8/3. This is an average: Fe₃O₄ is FeO·Fe₂O₃ with one Fe²⁺ and two Fe³⁺.

questions.q: Oxidation number of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH, is
questions.x: In metal hydrides hydrogen is bonded to a less electronegative metal, so it takes −1 (Na is +1).
questions.trap: +1: applying the usual rule for H without the metal-hydride exception.

questions.q: Which species can act ONLY as an oxidising agent?
questions.x: N in HNO₃ is +5, its highest oxidation state, so it can only be reduced. HNO₂ (N +3), H₂O₂ (O −1) and SO₂ (S +4) are intermediate and can go both ways.

questions.q: In the reaction CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, the substance that is reduced is
questions.x: Classically, reduction is removal of oxygen: CuO loses oxygen to become Cu. H₂ gains oxygen and is oxidised.
questions.trap: H₂: it is the reducing agent, which is itself oxidised.

questions.q: Which reaction is a disproportionation reaction?
questions.x: In H₂O₂, oxygen (−1) is simultaneously reduced to −2 (H₂O) and oxidised to 0 (O₂): the same element goes both ways.

questions.q: In acidic medium, Cr₂O₇²⁻ oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ and is itself reduced to Cr³⁺. Moles of Fe²⁺ oxidised by one mole of Cr₂O₇²⁻ are
questions.x: Each Cr goes +6 → +3 (gains 3e⁻); two Cr gain 6e⁻. Each Fe²⁺ loses 1e⁻, so 6 Fe²⁺ per Cr₂O₇²⁻.
questions.trap: 3: counting only one Cr atom.

questions.q: An open vessel contains air at 27 °C. It is heated to 127 °C at constant pressure. The fraction of the original air that remains in the vessel is
questions.x: At fixed P and V, n ∝ 1/T. n₂/n₁ = 300/400 = 3/4 remains (1/4 escapes).
questions.trap: 1/4: that is the fraction that escapes.

questions.q: A gas diffuses 4 times more slowly than hydrogen under the same conditions. Its molar mass is
questions.x: Graham's law: r(H₂)/r = √(M/2) = 4 → M = 16 × 2 = 32 g mol⁻¹.
questions.trap: 8: forgetting to square the rate ratio.

questions.q: 100 mL of O₂ effuses through a pinhole in 20 s. Under the same conditions, 100 mL of H₂ will effuse in
questions.trap: 80 s: taking time inversely proportional to √M.

questions.q: Dalton's law of partial pressures does NOT apply to a mixture of
o: H₂ and O₂ at room temperature
questions.x: The law holds only for non-reacting gases. NH₃ and HCl react at once to form solid NH₄Cl.
questions.trap: H₂ and O₂: they do not react at room temperature without a spark.

questions.q: A gas can be liquefied by applying pressure alone only when it is
o: at any temperature if the pressure is high enough
questions.x: Above the critical temperature no pressure, however high, can liquefy a gas.

questions.q: Equal masses of methane and oxygen are mixed in an empty vessel. The fraction of the total pressure exerted by oxygen is
questions.x: Moles: O₂ = m/32, CH₄ = m/16 = 2m/32. Mole fraction of O₂ = 1/(1 + 2) = 1/3 = fraction of pressure.
questions.trap: 1/2: assuming equal masses give equal pressures.

questions.q: In a cubic crystal, atoms A occupy the corners and atoms B occupy the face centres. The formula of the compound is
questions.x: A: 8 corners × 1/8 = 1. B: 6 faces × 1/2 = 3. Formula AB₃.
questions.trap: AB₆: counting each face-centre atom as wholly inside the cell.

questions.q: Coordination number of an atom in a body-centred cubic (bcc) lattice is
questions.x: The body-centre atom touches the 8 corner atoms. Simple cubic = 6, fcc = 12.

questions.q: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), increasing the pressure
o: shifts the equilibrium backward and decreases the dissociation of PCl₅
has no effect on the equilibrium
questions.x: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles: 1 mol (left) against 2 mol (right).

questions.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), increasing the total pressure
questions.x: Both sides have 2 mol of gas (Δn = 0), so pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium.

questions.q: An inert gas such as argon is added to an equilibrium mixture of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ at constant volume. The equilibrium
o: shifts in a direction depending on ΔH
questions.x: At constant volume the partial pressures (concentrations) of the reacting gases do not change, so Q still equals K.
questions.trap: Shifts forward: treating the higher total pressure as if it compressed the reactants.

questions.q: Kp equals Kc for a gaseous reaction when
questions.x: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn; when Δn = 0, (RT)⁰ = 1, so Kp = Kc (e.g. H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI).

questions.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), Kc = 100 at a certain temperature. At the same temperature, Kc for SO₃(g) ⇌ SO₂(g) + ½O₂(g) is
questions.x: Reversing gives 1/100; halving the coefficients takes the square root: √(1/100) = 0.1.
questions.trap: 0.01: reversing the reaction but forgetting to take the square root.

questions.q: For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI in a 1 L flask, the equilibrium amounts are 0.1 mol H₂, 0.1 mol I₂ and 0.8 mol HI. Kc is
questions.trap: 80: forgetting to square [HI].

questions.q: For ice ⇌ water, increasing the pressure
o: raises the melting point of ice
questions.x: Water occupies less volume than ice, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium toward water; the melting point of ice falls.

questions.q: The equilibrium constant of a given reaction changes when
o: the concentration of a reactant is changed
questions.x: K depends only on temperature. Changes of concentration or pressure shift the position, not K; a catalyst changes neither.

questions.q: Drinking water contains 5 ppm of fluoride. Mass of fluoride in 2 kg of this water is
Concentrated HCl is 36.5% HCl by mass and has density 1.2 g mL⁻¹. Its molarity is
questions.trap: 10 M: ignoring the density (taking 1 L = 1000 g).

questions.q: Equivalent weight of KMnO₄ (M = 158) when it is reduced to MnO₂ in neutral medium is about
questions.x: Mn goes +7 → +4, gaining 3 electrons: n-factor 3. Equivalent weight = 158/3 = 52.7.
questions.trap: 31.6: that is in acidic medium (n-factor 5).

questions.q: Volume of 0.1 M KMnO₄ needed to oxidise 50 mL of 0.5 M FeSO₄ in acidic medium is
questions.x: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ → … Fe²⁺ = 0.025 mol, so MnO₄⁻ = 0.005 mol; V = 0.005/0.1 L = 50 mL.
questions.trap: 250 mL: treating KMnO₄ and Fe²⁺ as reacting 1 : 1.

questions.q: Volume of water to be added to 100 mL of 0.5 M HCl to make it 0.1 M is
questions.x: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂: 0.5 × 100 = 0.1 × V₂ → V₂ = 500 mL. Water added = 500 − 100 = 400 mL.
questions.trap: 500 mL: that is the final volume, not the water added.

questions.q: Molality is preferred to molarity for precise work because molality
o: is based on the volume of solution
does not depend on the mass of solute
questions.x: Molality uses mass of solvent, which does not change with temperature; molarity uses volume, which expands on heating.

questions.q: Normality of 0.3 M H₃PO₄ when it is completely neutralised by NaOH is
questions.x: Complete neutralisation replaces all 3 H⁺ (basicity 3). N = M × n-factor = 0.3 × 3 = 0.9 N.

questions.q: When solid NH₄Cl is added to a solution of NH₄OH
o: the pH of the solution rises
NH₃ gas is evolved at once
the ionisation of NH₄OH is suppressed and [OH⁻] decreases
questions.x: NH₄⁺ is a common ion; it pushes NH₄OH ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ backward (common ion effect), lowering [OH⁻] and pH.

questions.q: Which species is amphiprotic (can both donate and accept a proton)?
questions.x: HCO₃⁻ gives H⁺ to form CO₃²⁻ and accepts H⁺ to form H₂CO₃. CO₃²⁻ and Cl⁻ only accept; NH₄⁺ only donates.

questions.q: pH of 0.01 M NaOH solution at 25 °C is
questions.x: [OH⁻] = 10⁻² M, so pOH = 2 and pH = 14 − 2 = 12.
questions.trap: 2: that is the pOH, not the pH.

questions.q: Degree of ionisation of 0.1 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) is about
Ksp of Mg(OH)₂ is 4 × 10⁻¹². Its solubility in pure water is
questions.x: Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³ = 4 × 10⁻¹² → s³ = 10⁻¹² → s = 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹.
questions.trap: 2 × 10⁻⁶: using s = √Ksp, which applies only to AB-type salts.

questions.q: When pure water is heated from 25 °C to 60 °C, its pH
o: falls below 7, but the water remains neutral
falls below 7 and the water becomes acidic
rises above 7 and the water becomes basic
questions.x: Ionisation of water is endothermic, so Kw increases with temperature: [H⁺] rises and pH falls, but [H⁺] = [OH⁻] still, so it is neutral.
questions.trap: Becomes acidic: equating pH < 7 with acidity at every temperature.

questions.q: An aqueous solution of sodium acetate is
questions.x: Salt of a weak acid and a strong base: CH₃COO⁻ hydrolyses (CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻), so the solution is basic.

questions.q: For 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. If [NO] is doubled and [O₂] is halved, the rate becomes
questions.x: New rate = k(2[NO])²(½[O₂]) = 4 × ½ = 2 times the original.
questions.trap: 4 times: changing [NO] but ignoring the halving of [O₂].

questions.q: Unit of the rate constant of a zero-order reaction is
questions.x: Units of k = (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) s⁻¹; for n = 0 this is mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, the same as the unit of rate.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 20 min. Time needed for 75% of it to react is
questions.x: 75% reacted = 25% left = (½)², i.e. two half-lives: 2 × 20 = 40 min.
questions.trap: 30 min: scaling 75% linearly from the half-life.

questions.q: According to the Arrhenius equation k = Ae^(−Ea/RT), a plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with slope
questions.x: ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T): slope −Ea/R, intercept ln A. (−Ea/2.303R is the slope for log k.)
questions.trap: −Ea/2.303R: that is for log₁₀ k, not ln k.

questions.q: For the reaction 2A → B, the rates of change of concentration are related by
questions.x: Rate = −½ d[A]/dt = d[B]/dt, so A disappears twice as fast as B forms: −d[A]/dt = 2 d[B]/dt.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has k = 2.303 × 10⁻² s⁻¹. Time taken for the reactant to fall to one-tenth of its initial value is
questions.trap: 30.1 s: that is the half-life, not the time to reach 1/10.

questions.q: Standard reduction potentials: Mg²⁺/Mg −2.37 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V, Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V. The strongest oxidising agent among the ions is
questions.x: The most positive reduction potential means the greatest tendency to be reduced, so Ag⁺ is the strongest oxidant (Mg is the strongest reductant).
questions.trap: Mg²⁺: confusing strongest reducing metal (Mg) with strongest oxidising ion.

questions.q: Galvanisation protects iron from rusting by coating it with
questions.x: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so even if scratched it corrodes first (sacrificial protection). Tin plating is called tinning.

questions.q: In a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an alkaline (KOH) electrolyte, the reaction at the cathode is
questions.x: Reduction occurs at the cathode: oxygen takes electrons and, in alkali, forms OH⁻. H₂ is oxidised at the anode; overall product is water.
questions.trap: H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻: that is the anode (oxidation).

questions.q: One faraday is the quantity of electric charge carried by
o: one ampere flowing for one hour

questions.q: Volume of oxygen at STP liberated at the anode when 1 faraday of charge is passed through acidified water is
questions.x: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻: 4 F give 1 mol (22.4 L) O₂, so 1 F gives 22.4/4 = 5.6 L.
questions.trap: 11.2 L: that is the H₂ liberated at the cathode by 1 F.

questions.q: Rusting of iron needs
questions.x: Rusting is electrochemical oxidation of iron; iron kept in dry air or in boiled, oxygen-free water does not rust.

questions.q: A gas absorbs 10 J of heat and does 30 J of work on the surroundings. The change in its internal energy is
questions.x: ΔU = q + w with q = +10 J (absorbed) and w = −30 J (work done by the system). ΔU = 10 − 30 = −20 J.
questions.trap: +40 J: adding both without applying the sign convention.

questions.q: Standard enthalpies of formation: CH₄(g) −74.8, CO₂(g) −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy of combustion of methane is
questions.trap: −604.5: forgetting that two moles of water form.

questions.q: A reaction with ΔH negative and ΔS negative is spontaneous
questions.x: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔS < 0, −TΔS is positive and grows with T; ΔG stays negative only while T is low.

questions.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) at temperature T, ΔH − ΔU equals
questions.x: ΔH = ΔU + Δn(gas)RT; Δn = 2 − 4 = −2, so ΔH − ΔU = −2RT.
questions.trap: +2RT: taking Δn as reactants minus products.

questions.q: SI unit of molar entropy is
questions.x: Entropy change = heat absorbed reversibly/temperature, so its unit is J K⁻¹; per mole, J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: The enthalpy of combustion of a substance is always
o: positive for gases and negative for solids
questions.x: Combustion releases heat (exothermic), so ΔH of combustion is always negative.

questions.q: Complete the reaction: ²⁷₁₃Al + ¹₀n → ²⁴₁₁Na + ?
questions.x: Mass: 27 + 1 = 24 + A → A = 4. Charge: 13 + 0 = 11 + Z → Z = 2. The particle is ⁴₂He.

questions.q: In the fission ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n, the value of x is
questions.x: Mass numbers: 235 + 1 = 141 + 92 + x → x = 3. Atomic numbers balance: 92 = 56 + 36.
questions.trap: 2: forgetting the incoming neutron on the left side.

questions.q: ²³²₉₀Th decays to ²⁰⁸₈₂Pb. The numbers of α- and β-particles emitted are
questions.x: α count = (232 − 208)/4 = 6, lowering Z by 12 to 78. To reach 82, Z must rise by 4: 4 β-particles.

questions.q: A β-particle is
o: a fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus
questions.x: β-decay: a neutron changes into a proton and an electron; the electron is ejected as the β-particle.

questions.q: The radioisotope commonly used as a γ-ray source in radiotherapy of cancer is
questions.x: Co-60 emits strong γ-rays used to destroy cancer cells. C-14 is used in dating; Na-24 traces blood flow.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits a positron (⁰₊₁e)
o: its atomic number increases by 1 and its mass number is unchanged
its atomic number decreases by 1 and its mass number is unchanged
its atomic number decreases by 2 and its mass number by 4
both the atomic number and mass number are unchanged
questions.x: A proton becomes a neutron plus a positron, so Z falls by 1 while A stays the same.
questions.trap: Increases by 1: confusing positron emission with β⁻ emission.

questions.q: Steam distillation is suitable for purifying
questions.x: Steam distillation suits liquids that are steam-volatile and immiscible with water, like aniline. Glycerol needs vacuum distillation.
questions.trap: Glycerol: it decomposes at its boiling point and needs reduced-pressure distillation.

questions.q: Differential (solvent) extraction separates a compound because it
o: has a lower boiling point than water
forms a precipitate with the solvent
is more soluble in an organic solvent that is immiscible with water
questions.x: The compound distributes between two immiscible liquids; it passes into the solvent in which it is more soluble, which is then separated in a separating funnel.

questions.q: A mixture of chloroform (b.p. 61 °C) and aniline (b.p. 184 °C) is best separated by
questions.x: The boiling points differ widely, so the more volatile chloroform distils off first in a simple distillation.
questions.trap: Fractional distillation: needed only when boiling points are close.

questions.q: In column (adsorption) chromatography, the stationary phase is usually
questions.x: The mixture is adsorbed on a column of alumina or silica gel; components are eluted by the solvent (mobile phase) at different rates.

questions.q: In a paper chromatogram the solvent front moved 12 cm and a spot moved 3 cm. The Rf value of the spot is
questions.x: Rf = distance moved by substance/distance moved by solvent = 3/12 = 0.25.
questions.trap: 4: dividing the solvent distance by the spot distance.

questions.q: Two immiscible liquids such as oil and water are separated using a
questions.x: Immiscible liquids form two layers; the lower layer is run off through the tap of a separating funnel.

questions.q: Na₂CO₃ solution is titrated with HCl using phenolphthalein. The end point corresponds to
o: conversion of Na₂CO₃ to NaCl, CO₂ and H₂O
the first drop of HCl added
questions.x: Phenolphthalein turns colourless near pH 8.3, when Na₂CO₃ + HCl → NaHCO₃ + NaCl (half neutralisation). Methyl orange marks complete neutralisation.
questions.trap: Complete conversion to CO₂: that end point needs methyl orange.

questions.q: In the titration of Fe²⁺ with K₂Cr₂O₇, the indicator used is
questions.x: K₂Cr₂O₇ is not a self-indicator, so an internal redox indicator, diphenylamine (violet-blue at the end point), is used.

questions.q: In Mohr's method, chloride ions are titrated with AgNO₃ using
questions.x: After all Cl⁻ precipitates as white AgCl, excess Ag⁺ forms red-brown Ag₂CrO₄, marking the end point of this precipitation titration.

questions.q: At the equivalence point of a strong acid–strong base titration at 25 °C, the pH of the solution is
questions.x: The salt formed (e.g. NaCl) does not hydrolyse, so the solution is neutral, pH 7.

questions.q: CaCO₃ in limestone is estimated by adding a known excess of standard HCl and titrating the unused acid with standard NaOH. This is
questions.x: Insoluble or slowly reacting samples are treated with excess reagent; the excess is then titrated, and the difference gives the amount reacted.

questions.q: Methyl orange is NOT suitable for titrating acetic acid with NaOH because
o: it changes colour (pH 3.1–4.4) well before the equivalence point, which lies near pH 8–9
it is reduced by acetic acid
it changes colour only above pH 10
questions.x: The equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration is basic, so phenolphthalein (8.3–10) is used; methyl orange turns too early.

questions.q: In the Victor Meyer test, a secondary alcohol gives
questions.x: Victor Meyer test: primary → blood red, secondary → blue, tertiary → colourless.
questions.trap: Blood red: that is the primary alcohol result.

questions.q: Which compound does NOT decolourise Baeyer's reagent?
questions.x: Baeyer's reagent (cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄) is decolourised by C=C and C≡C; benzene's stable aromatic ring does not react.
questions.trap: Treating benzene's ring 'double bonds' as ordinary alkene bonds.

questions.q: Which acid gives a positive Tollens' (silver mirror) test?
questions.x: Formic acid, H–COOH, contains an aldehyde-like –CHO group and reduces ammoniacal AgNO₃ to silver. Other carboxylic acids do not.
